passage:
Week one. Manjula sat on the bench in her knee brace while the kabaddi team trained without her. Swati took her raiding spot and scored twice. Manjula went home, barely spoke and stared at the ceiling. Who am I if I'm not a raider?
Week three. Coach asked her to keep the team's stats and still come to every practice. Manjula grumbled, but she came. At home she took out her old sketchbook for the first time in a year and drew the team in the middle of a raid.
Week six. She did the exercises the physio had shown her, every evening, even the boring ones. At the district match she sat by the court with her clipboard and cheered loudest when Swati scored. Her knee felt stronger. So did she.

qa.q: What did Coach ask Manjula to keep?
qa.a: Coach asked her to keep the team's stats.

qa.q: What was Manjula afraid of in week one?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing her place and her sense of who she was, since Swati had taken her raiding spot.

qa.q: What choices protected Manjula's mind during recovery?
qa.a: Staying part of the team, returning to her drawing, and doing her physio exercises regularly.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Manjula cheers loudest for her?
qa.a: Swati probably feels relieved and supported, knowing Manjula is not resentful.

grounding: It shows a teenage athlete sidelined by injury feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and how staying with the team, other interests and following advice help.

passage:
Aadhya, you think you're the first girl to be benched? Listen to your Sudha Masi. When I was sixteen, I ran the eight hundred metres for our district. Then my ankle twisted in a pothole, two weeks before the state meet.
I cried for days. A younger girl, Leela, took my spot. I was sure the coach had forgotten me. I stopped going to the ground. I told everyone I didn't care about running anymore.
Then my coach came to our house. She said, "I need a timekeeper, and I need you back when you're healed. Do what the doctor says and don't rush." So I kept time with a stopwatch every morning. I also joined the school choir to fill my evenings.
The next season I ran again. Leela and I became training partners.
So don't give up on your team.

qa.q: What job did the coach give Sudha while she healed?
qa.a: The coach made her the timekeeper.

qa.q: How did the young Sudha feel when Leela took her spot?
qa.a: She felt lost and afraid of being forgotten, so she cried and pretended she no longer cared about running.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sudha's story?
qa.a: The coach's visit, which brought her back as timekeeper while she followed the doctor's advice and found singing too.

qa.q: How might Leela have seen the young Sudha coming back as timekeeper?
qa.a: Leela may have felt less awkward and more welcome, which helped them later become training partners.

grounding: It shows a teenage athlete sidelined by injury feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and staying connected to the team and other interests while healing.

passage: In the sports hostel in Bhopal, Simran, sixteen, lay on her bed with her knee in a brace. A ligament tear in the state hockey final meant months without playing. Through the window she could hear the team at practice, the clack of sticks, and felt like a ghost. Hockey was who she was. What if Coach picked someone else for her position? She stopped going to the canteen. Then Coach Leela knocked. 'You're still on this team. I need someone to track passes and tackles at every match. Will you do it?' Simran hesitated. 'I can't even walk properly.' 'You can sit and watch. And you'll do every physio exercise the doctor gave you.' Simran went to the next match with a notebook. The girls cheered when she arrived.

qa.q: What did Coach Leela ask Simran to track?
qa.a: Passes and tackles at every match.

qa.q: What was Simran afraid of while injured?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing her place and her identity, feeling like a ghost cut off from the team.

qa.q: What did Coach Leela do to protect Simran's mind and recovery?
qa.a: She kept Simran part of the team with a real job and made sure she followed the doctor's physio plan.

qa.q: How might the girls on the team have felt when Simran arrived?
qa.a: They were glad and happy to see her, cheering her arrival.

grounding: Shows an injured teenage athlete feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and how staying part of the team and following medical advice protect her mind and recovery.

passage:
Dear Farhan Sir,
I'm writing because I haven't been to the club since the doctor said my shoulder needs three months off. I know you messaged. I just didn't know what to say.
Badminton has been my whole life since I was nine. Without it I don't know who I am. I keep thinking you'll give my place to Aisha and forget about me. Some days I just stay in bed.
My Ammi says I should still come on Saturdays. Could I help with the juniors, or keep scores? I'm also doing the physio exercises every morning, like the doctor said, and I've started drawing again, which I used to love.
Please tell me honestly if there's still a place for me.
Hafsa

qa.q: How long does Hafsa's shoulder need off?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: What does Hafsa feel since the injury?
qa.a: Hafsa feels lost and low, afraid of being replaced and forgotten.

qa.q: What steps is Hafsa taking to protect body and mind?
qa.a: Offering to help with juniors or keep scores, doing physio every morning, and drawing again.

qa.q: How might Farhan Sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Farhan Sir is likely to feel moved and eager to reassure Hafsa of a place at the club.

grounding: Shows an injured teenage athlete feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and staying involved, keeping other interests and following medical advice.

passage: Okay, Sarita, you asked for the real story on the school podcast. I'm Dilnaz, and last year I got a stress fracture in my foot, two weeks before the district cross-country. For months, running was my entire identity. I was 'Dilnaz the runner'. Suddenly I was just… Dilnaz with a boot. I felt empty. I scrolled through the team's photos and cried. I was terrified someone faster would take my spot. What helped? My coach made me keep coming to training to time the others. I went every day, even in the boot. I did every physio exercise, boring as they were. And I joined the science club, which I'd always wanted to try, and it turns out I love it. I'm running again now. But I'm not only a runner any more, and that feels safer.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz get the stress fracture?
qa.a: In the foot.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel after the injury?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt empty and lost, terrified of losing the team spot.

qa.q: What three things helped Dilnaz?
qa.a: Staying part of training by timing others, doing the physio exercises and joining the science club.

qa.q: How might the team have seen Dilnaz timing their runs?
qa.a: The team probably saw someone still committed to them and felt glad Dilnaz stayed involved.

grounding: Shows an injured teenage athlete losing a sense of identity and fearing replacement, and how staying with the team, other interests and medical advice protect mind and recovery.

passage:
Week one: Gargi watched the district hockey trials from the stands with her knee in a brace. When the coach put Aditi in her position, Gargi went home and didn't touch her phone all evening. "Who am I if I'm not playing?" she wrote in her notebook.
Week three: Aditi texted, "We need someone to track the other team's corners. Coach asked for you." Gargi went, clipboard in hand, and found she liked spotting patterns. She also did every exercise the doctor had set, even the boring ones.
Week seven: Back on the field for light drills, Gargi saw Aditi still in her spot. It stung. But at the break Aditi said, "Your corner notes won us the semi." Gargi grinned.

qa.q: What job did the coach ask Gargi to do in week three?
qa.a: Tracking the other team's corners.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling in week one, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt lost, low and afraid of being replaced; she ignored her phone and wrote, "Who am I if I'm not playing?"

qa.q: What helped Gargi through the injury?
qa.a: Staying part of the team through the corner notes, finding a new interest in spotting patterns, and doing every exercise the doctor set.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel about taking Gargi's position?
qa.a: Aditi may feel a little awkward about it, which could be why she keeps including Gargi and praises her notes.

grounding: Shows a teenage athlete sidelined by injury feeling lost and afraid of being replaced, and staying part of the team, a new interest and medical advice protecting her.
